The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."
As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued...without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."
However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.
"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

blocks.caption: Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev have a daughter togetherImage: Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: "We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.
However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."
Zverev's lawyers: 'permissible expression of opinion'
Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.
"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.
Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.

blocks.caption: This year, Alexander Zverev became Germany's first men's No. 1 player since Boris BeckerImage: Michael Baucher/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."
The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."
Patea's lawyer: 'We had no choice' but court
Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.
"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.
"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."
Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

articles.title: AI demand will push up interest rates around the world, IMF head warns
articles.summary: Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’

blocks.text: Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.
Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.
She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.
“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Central banks have been forced to raise interest rates this year after the outbreak of war in February drove the global oil price above $100 a barrel, reigniting inflationary pressures around the world. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by the US Federal Reserve in September and the Bank of England earlier this month.
Financial markets expect further increases in the cost of borrowing next year, as the rapid rollout of AI bolsters economic growth against the volatile backdrop of the conflict.

However, global oil prices have fallen back in recent weeks, following the US midterm elections and an upswing in the supply of crude. Fears about an AI bubble and febrile conditions in global equity markets could dent business investment, and economists warn of a slowdown in demand as high inflation squeezes households.
Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”
after newsletter promotion
Georgieva’s comments came a day after the ECB warned about the rising amount of debt that AI companies are taking on to fuel their growth.

The central bank said there were “historic parallels” with the dotcom bubble that led to a tech market crash at the turn of the millennium, as well as the sub-prime mortgage bubble that triggered the 2008 financial crisis. It said in its financial stability review that any fallout from an AI crash “could lead to spillovers affecting euro area financial stability”.

For now, at least, the sector is still booming. Thursday marked a pivotal day for AI, as Anthropic debuted on the US stock market, raising the largest investment of any initial public offering after pricing at $83 per share.

The company, which makes the AI chatbot Claude, is expected to become one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world at $1.5tn, despite reporting $80bn worth of losses in the first half of 2026.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 44: Defense witness scrutinized, flame transition removed
articles.summary: The 43rd day of Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial saw the House prosecution and defense counsel clash over the capacity of witness AML Consulting PH founder Rainer Dela Fuente to answer…

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 11:06pm

The 43rd day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial saw the House prosecution and defense counsel clash over the capacity of witness AML Consulting PH founder Rainer Dela Fuente to answer questions.

The beginning of the trial, however, was marked by a strange moment wherein during the prayer of Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano, there was a flame transition during the livestream. The moment caught the attention of netizens online, with many finding the mishap comedic.

The trial opened with an unusual moment when a flame transition appeared on the livestream while Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano was leading the prayer. The unexpected visual caught the attention of netizens, many of whom found the livestream mishap amusing.

Senate impeachment presiding officer Francis Escudero later ordered the transition edited out of the livestream, with the Senate Public Relations and Information Bureau (PRIB) apologizing for the incident.
Defense counsel Mark Vinluan presented Dela Fuente, a CPA lawyer and former investigator for the Anti-Money Laundering Council.

House prosecutor Chel Diokno objected to Dela Fuente being a witness, pointing out that Duterte was not facing a charge of money laundering. Vinluan argued that there was a portion of the impeachment article stating that there may have been money laundering. =
Escudero said that the defense had leeway in presenting evidence.

Vinluan presented various clips of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the late senator Miriam Defensor-Santiago, and the late Chief Justice Renato Corona, asking Dela Fuente for his opinions on their statements.
Diokno objected to the line of questioning, with several senator-judges raising concerns about presenting video statements from people who could not be questioned.
Vinuluan also quizzed Dela Fuente on portions of financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera’s report, which alleged that Duterte had unexplained wealth amounting to P817 million.

The matter of Dela Fuente’s capacity to answer questions became a running question among the prosecution and the senator-judges, especially when it was revealed that Dela Fuente did not even read Cabrera’s report. Neither did he read the impeachment articles nor other evidence presented before the court.

Dela Fuente would later clarify that he was not discounting Cabrera’s report, as he was only asked hypothetical questions. He maintained that he could only compare the portions being presented to him with the law.

On other matters, Escudero allowed the witness from the Center for International Expositions and Missions (CITEM), department manager Rowena Mendoza, to be replaced by CITEM chief of Corporate Planning Eva Marie Mariquina. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Four UK men convicted of sexual assault and rape of woman at invitation of husband
articles.summary:
Former Tory councillor advertised ex-wife on swinging websites and drugged and bound her for sex

Four men have been convicted of sexually assaulting and raping a woman at the invitation of…

blocks.text: Four men have been convicted of sexually assaulting and raping a woman at the invitation of her husband who had drugged and bound her.

Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” where anything could be done to her by whoever answered the adverts, jurors were told.
The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.
Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32; Richard Wilkins, 62; Norman Macksoni, 48; and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were convicted of various offences against Joanne Young after a three-week trial.

Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor from Swindon, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration; Wilkins, a taxi driver from Swindon, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape; Macksoni, a former DJ and waste management worker from Bedfordshire, was convicted of rape; and Hassan, also from Swindon, was found guilty of sexual assault.
A further defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, from Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.

The case has drawn comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged by her husband and raped by dozens of strangers in France. It can now be revealed that Wiltshire police received advice from the Pelicot investigators on how to approach their inquiries.
The men, including Young, will be sentenced together at a later date.

articles.title: EU Commission confirms it was targeted in cyberattack using AI tools
articles.summary: The European Commission was targeted by an "AI-generated cybercampaign," a spokesperson has said. This is the first time the bloc has publicly reported an AI-based cyberattack.

image.caption: This is the first time the European Union reported an AI-assisted cyberattackImage: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

blocks.text: The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was ‌targeted by ⁠a ⁠cyberattack through the use of AI tools.
The incident was detected on October 22 and there was ‌no evidence ​of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.
"This was an AI-generated ‌cybercampaign," he added.
Regnier did not elaborate on the attack or name a perpetrator. He said the Commission "has taken the necessary steps in response."
This is the first time the bloc reported an AI-assisted cyberattack.
Disruption reportedly lasted 10 days

Regnier's statement came after Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission had been targeted. The report said the cyberattack disrupted several systems for 10 days and might have compromised large amounts of personal data. The European Commission has roughly 33,000 employees.
Are humans becoming too attached to AI?
The ​Commission then convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents, according to Politico.

"We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. He also stated that they did not detect any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.

Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets, air traffic controllers, blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries among leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.
France summoned the Iranian ambassador last week over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.
Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments?

articles.title: Language issues continue to dog accused murderer’s court appearances in N.L.
articles.summary: A Quebec man accused of first-degree murder in Happy Valley-Goose Bay, N.L., continues to experience problems after electing to have his case tried in French, including a Crown prosecutor not…

image.caption: A judge at Wabush provincial court has presided over Dave Faucher's court appearances this fall. The Quebec accused of first-degree murder has elected for the proceedings to occur in French. (Darryl Dinn/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

A Quebec man accused of first-degree murder in Happy Valley-Goose Bay, N.L., continues to experience problems after electing to have his case tried in French, including a Crown prosecutor not comfortable speaking “legal French,” and issues with members in the courtroom being able to understand an interpreter.
Interpreter unable to translate key word during Dave Faucher’s most recent hearing
Language issues continue to dog the court appearances of a Quebecer accused of first-degree murder in Happy Valley-Goose Bay, N.L., who elected for his case to be heard in French.

While a previous hearing made headlines when a Crown prosecutor said he didn’t feel comfortable speaking “legal French” before a judge, Dave Faucher’s latest provincial court appearance on Oct. 27 featured an interpreter who was unable to translate the word “divulgation” into English.

“Divulgation” is the French word for “disclosure.” Given the nearly 15-minute hearing focused almost entirely on evidence disclosure timelines, the Crown eventually felt it necessary to correct the interpreter, who was participating remotely.
“‘Disclosure’, the word is ‘disclosure,’” said prosecutor Mary Bellefleur, a francophone Crown appointed to the case last month.

Meanwhile, Judge Wynne Anne Trahey complained during the same hearing that it was difficult to understand the interpreter, who participated by distance and whose voice boomed from a loud speaker in the Wabush courtroom.
“The sound is not good,” said the judge, adding at one point that the clerk “didn’t understand anything” the interpreter was saying.
English interpretation appears to have been offered given the clerk and the family of Franz Drosch, the man Faucher is accused of killing in 2023, didn’t speak French.

items: N.L. prosecutors unable to speak French during court appearances of man accused of murder
David Faucher makes brief court appearance in Labrador on 1st-degree murder charge

blocks.text: No certification process for interpreters

The interpreter for the Oct. 27 court appearance was provided by the Association for New Canadians, whose spokesperson David Slavick wouldn’t speak to individual workers’ qualifications but confirmed “there is no formal certification process for interpreters in Newfoundland and Labrador.”
Joanne Turner, the CEO of the provincial and Supreme courts, said “there is no one consistent certification training or process due to the hundreds of languages and dialects necessary.
Long-time interpreter Jeff Staflund said that’s not quite the case.

“Standards exist, but they’re not upheld,” said Staflund, who helped establish a legal interpreter training program at Université Sainte-Anne in Nova Scotia. “Interpretation isn’t a regulated profession either, so there’s no legal requirement to verify whether someone has passed the national certification exam.”
Jeff Staflund is a long-time translator and court interpreter based in Winnipeg. (Jeff Staflund)

“It’s the agencies who hire us and the organizations that require our services that need to make sure standards are met,” added Sheila Hussain, the president of the Ontario Court Interpreters’ Association.

For interpretation in the country’s two official languages, there is a healthy pool of interpreters in provinces such as Manitoba and New Brunswick, according to Staflund. He said New Brunswick has a uniform training and exam process, but described interpretation services in most of the country’s courts as the “wild west.”

“People don’t understand the difficulty of the work. They think that anyone who is bilingual can perform this task, when it takes quite intensive training and skills that go beyond the simple ability to speak two languages,” said the former head interpreter for New Brunswick, now based in Winnipeg.
Justice minister ‘unable to comment’

In the Faucher appearances to date, consecutive interpretation has been offered. When consecutive interpretation is used, the speaker — whether the judge, a lawyer or a witness — expresses one thought at a time, then waits while the interpreter steps in to translate.
While consecutive interpretation can sometimes prove painfully slow, it is the translation method most commonly used in Canadian courts, according to Staflund.

Asked whether she had concerns about the quality of interpretation in the Faucher case, and in the province’s court system more generally, Justice and Public Safety Minister Helen Conway Ottenheimer declined to comment.
Helen Conway Ottenheimer is the province's justice and public safety minister. (Ryan Cooke/CBC)

“The questions posed relate to ongoing court proceedings; therefore, in my role as minister of Justice and Public Safety and Attorney General, I am unable to comment,” reads a statement from Conway Ottenheimer provided by spokesperson Vaughn Hammond.
“Concerning the interpretation services provided by the provincial court, these are operational matters and, as such, any questions should be directed to the provincial court.”

Turner said the courts she oversees hire their interpreters through the ANC but also the province’s Francophone federation and several Indigenous band councils. When local interpreters aren’t available, they work with “a number of companies” elsewhere in the country to find the staff they need.
Quality interpretation essential, says expert
Staflund said he recognized that ensuring consistent, high-quality court interpretation isn't an easy task.

He said training programs are too few and often too expensive. He also said interpreters often aren’t paid enough and that the relatively low demand for interpretation services in provinces such as Newfoundland and Labrador makes it difficult to gain experience and maintain stable hours.
However, Staflund said reliable, accurate court interpreters are essential to a functioning court system.
“The accused and the witnesses need to be understood and need to understand,” he said.
Faucher's next court appearance is Friday.
Trahey is hearing the case because there is no available bilingual judge in Happy Valley-Goose Bay.

articles.title: Top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Muslim Rohingya
articles.summary: 'The court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children...'…

blocks.text: ROHINGYA. Rohingya refugee children react as the verdict is translated for the gathered crowd watching the live announcement by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingya population, on a big screen at a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, November 19, 2026.
REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain

'The court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children...' Presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa says

items: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar's military committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority in 2017, marking a significant legal precedent.
The court found Myanmar responsible for mass killings, sexual violence, and destruction of villages, and ordered compensation and guarantees for the Rohingya's safe return.
This ruling is expected to influence future genocide cases and highlights the challenges of enforcing international law, as Myanmar denies the allegations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

THE HAGUE, Netherlands – The United Nations’ highest court ruled on Thursday, November 19, that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The decision, seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met. It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.

“The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya,” Presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.
The panel found “that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State.”

For the 1.2 million Rohingya forced into exile in the sprawling Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where more than 1,000 people cheered as the verdict came in on a TV screen, it was a historic moment of truth and vindication, a prominent Rohingya campaigner said.

“For decades, the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence, and dismiss our suffering,” said Wai Wai Nu, executive director of the Women’s Peace Network and a former political prisoner.

“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie.”
Myanmar’s government, which has denied genocide, saying its forces were tackling a violent insurgency, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.

blocks.caption: FAST FACTS: Who are the Rohingya?

blocks.text: Judges found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called clearance operations. The military actively spread hate speech targeting the Rohingya population, they said.
The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
Genocide has rarely been established in international courts, largely because prosecutors must prove a specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
The decision by the International Court of Justice, or World Court, is expected to have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, including for South Africa’s 2023 case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
Both Israel and Myanmar deny genocide and say their forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups.

The first major decision by the court in more than a decade on the application of the 1948 Genocide Convention will be pored over by legal experts for clues to how the bench assessed state responsibility in the alleged commission of international crimes.

In a major legal victory for Gambia, the court found the state responsible for genocide resulting from a military offensive that drove at least 700,000 Muslim Rohingya from Buddhist-majority Myanmar. The court adopted a UN fact-finding mission figure of at least 10,000 deaths during so-called clearance operations, saying it was supported by the record.

The court said “the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine state,” meeting the legal threshold for genocide.
The ruling said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined at a later date.
Myanmar must also allow the “safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts,” it said.

After losing everything, the Rohingya face struggles the court cannot solve, but the decision “will strengthen our efforts to return home,” said Sayed Ullah, a community representative speaking from Cox’s Bazar.

James Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, said that with growing pressure on international law and institutions upholding it, the ruling showed their vital role “in establishing truth, assigning responsibility, and protecting the values that bind our common humanity.”
International courts previously recognised genocide only in Rwanda in 1994, the 1995 Srebrenica killings in Bosnia, and atrocities by Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge in the late 1970s.
While rulings by the ICJ, which settles disputes between states and rules on alleged breaches of international treaties, are final, the court has very limited options to enforce them.

Former colonial ruler Britain said on Thursday that it was expelling Myanmar’s defense attache and would set out further action in coming days. Two British lawmakers urged the government to bring a resolution to the UN Security Council to compel enforcement action.
The ICJ is distinct from the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals for war crimes, crimes against ​humanity and genocide and can impose jail terms. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump takes 500 actions to weaken cancer protections, new report says
articles.summary:
Natural Resources Defense Council shows how federal rules changes will increase public’s exposure to carcinogens

Amid a

blocks.text: Amid a rise in early onset cancer, the Trump administration has taken more than 500 actions to systematically dismantle protections against carcinogens once in place across the federal government, an October report alleges.

The Natural Resources Defense Council report, and comments from current and former officials from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), brings into focus how myriad changes in federal rules or protocol will dramatically increase the public’s exposure to carcinogens. These are taking effect at a time when some forms of early onset cancer are spiking by about 30% per decade.

Some of the changes have drawn widespread outrage and backlash, including the administration delaying new protections around asbestos, or siding with Bayer in its fight to keep glyphosate, classified as a probable human carcinogen by an arm of the World Health Organization in 2015, on the market.

But most changes lie in the nuts and bolts of the federal government. These include alterations to important scientific processes that determine the level of risk people face in exposure to carcinogens. With a few minor adjustments, once-problematic levels of exposure to carcinogens, such as formaldehyde, are no longer considered a danger in the federal government’s eyes.

Other actions include the elimination of protective regulatory rules, the exploitation of presidential exemptions for polluters, the delay of new regulations already in motion, the elimination of research funding and wide-scale cuts to cancer research staff.

The actions amount to a “pro-cancer” agenda, the report states. NRDC lead author Erik Olson said he was “surprised by the breadth of the whole government effort to undermine all the protections against cancer”. It is not just the EPA, Olson said, but the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, independent commissions and many other governmental entities.

“The vast majority of people have no idea that this is happening because the Trump administration is mostly doing it without a lot of fanfare, so it’s hard to piece together this jigsaw puzzle, but we did and it shows a stark and shocking picture,” Olson said.
A White House spokesperson, Allison Schuster, said: “Make America Healthy Again was not just a campaign slogan – it was President Trump’s pledge to tackle America’s chronic disease epidemic.

“Delivering on this pledge has been a whole-of-government effort, and the White House’s launch of MAHA.gov transparently documents the Administration’s progress so far. President Trump will never stop fighting to empower Americans to take control of their health.”
An EPA spokesperson said the administration had delivered more than 500 environmental wins so far.

“The Trump EPA, as it has been since day one, is fully committed to fulfilling its core mission of protecting human health and the environment and has put the gold standard of science at every action it takes,” a spokesperson said.

Officials estimate there will be more than 2m US cancer diagnoses this year. People younger than 50 years old have experienced a nearly 3% increase in colon cancer rates each year from 2013 to 2022. More broadly, rates for 14 types of common cancers have jumped in recent decades, including a 35% increase in childhood leukemia.

The situation calls for more protections, but those rules, regulations and scientific processes that are most essential have long been on industry’s hitlist, said an EPA employee who declined to use their name for fear of retribution. Former industry officials are now running the EPA, and it is “horrifying to watch it all play out”, the employee said.

“It is coming from the top [of the agency], and they are being methodical, and doing a lot of damage to these very critical protection points, which is exactly what the chemical industry has wanted,” the employee said. “There is no way to sugarcoat what is happening.”

Among the most widely reverberating changes is the shift away from the “no safe level of exposure” principle that guided EPA science in developing protections for carcinogens. This works by assuming any level of exposure to carcinogens presents a risk, and the risk grows as the exposure dose grows.

The Trump EPA has started implementing a “threshold” approach in which it determines that some exposures to carcinogens is safe. This change has already resulted in weaker protections against formaldehyde, a toxicant widely used in consumer goods. The administration appears to be taking a similar approach to its regulation of hexavalent chromium, a widespread water contaminant.

Nuclear regulators are also eliminating the obligation to reduce exposure to radioactive carcinogens to the lowest reasonably achievable level, despite decades of scientific evidence that any level of radiation poses a cancer risk, the report states.

David Fotouhi, the second in command at the EPA, wrote in an early 2026 memo that the agency had been too conservative in estimating toxic chemicals’ health risks, including carcinogenicity. Those values should be revisited and loosened, Fatouhi suggested.

This undermines work on 500 risk assessments done since 1985 by the Integrated Risk Information System (Iris), the small EPA office that determines chemical toxicity. The changes to risk assessments are among the most pernicious Trump EPA moves because the findings underpin regulations that protect people from carcinogens in the air, water, consumer goods and elsewhere, said Betsy Southerland, a former water office director at the agency.
The change to the threshold approach is part of that, and the agency is also targeting a mechanism that protects children by factoring in an increased risk in their exposure to chemicals.

“This is a killer for any emerging contaminant work, and for [carcinogens and other chemicals] that they are revisiting,” Southerland said. The changes could also weaken cleanup requirements at Superfund sites, which is the designation for the nation’s most polluted areas, many of which contain cancer-linked substances.

The Trump EPA quietly loosened guidance around the type of studies required to set regulations around carcinogens, the report alleges. Long-term human or animal studies are the norm, but the agency now uses short-term modeling studies called new approach methodologies (Nams) that are known to be unreliable and easy to manipulate. A Nam study was used to weaken the risk assessment for p-DCB, a widely used consumer chemical that most regulatory agencies label a carcinogen.

Trump has also dramatically increased the use of “presidential pardons” for carcinogenic air pollution, which the report claims will increase exposure to arsenic, ethylene oxide and similar carcinogenic chemicals.

Meanwhile, the agency appears to be systematically using stall tactics via multiple channels to grind the regulatory process to a halt. For example, it delayed requirements for industry to provide cancer data for carcinogenic chemicals including benzene, bisphenol A and vinyl chloride, the building block for PVC material, which were supposed to be reviewed during the administration. It is unclear when this will happen.
Olson likened the situation to someone “dumping a huge dump truck full of termites on your house”.

“It’s not like any one termite is causing the house to collapse, but this is a totally intentional strategy of having innumerable termites eating away at the foundation of all our protections, and the house is going to collapse,” Olson said.

articles.title: Australian music industry rejects ‘divide and conquer’ proposal to give musicians exemption from AI scraping
articles.summary:
Reported proposal to give musicians special treatment is ‘unworkable’, Aria CEO says, vowing to stand with other creatives

  • Get our

blocks.text: The music industry will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.

The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.
The Albanese government would not comment on the reported proposal, but senior ministers have raised concerns about current copyright law in recent days, hinting reforms were needed.

Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), and Claire Pullen, the CEO of the Australian Writers’ Guild, said the creative community – which this week launched a major AI campaign – would remain united in rejecting such changes.
“I can’t see any creative workers leaving their colleagues behind,” Pullen said.

The Australian Financial Review reported on Thursday the government was considering a copyright change under which AI companies would buy permits to train on Australian content, but that music may be exempted. Such a proposal would be more in line with AI companies, after Anthropic suggested a model of “conditional approval” to scrape content unless a rightsholder objected, and OpenAI told a parliamentary committee it would “potentially” support paying into a fund for creators.

Guardian Australia was not able to independently verify details of the proposal. One senior member of the creative community, involved in copyright discussions with government, said they had heard some details of such an idea, but others said they had not and doubted the Albanese government would seriously entertain it. One source in the AI industry, who declined to be named, said they would welcome such a plan.

blocks.caption: Aria awards: how do Australian artists feel about their music being used to train AI? – video

blocks.text: Herd said she was unaware of the proposal before Thursday, but the music industry would not desert other creatives.
“Had we been consulted, we would have advised this scheme is unnecessary, unworkable and designed to suit the commercial interests of AI companies, not protect creators,” she told Guardian Australia.
“Our position is unchanged: we stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.”

Herd and Pullen said such a scheme would be difficult to implement technically, questioning how content like movies or TV shows – which combine copyrighted elements such as music, video and screenwriting – would be treated if just one element was exempted from AI scraping.

“This just seems like such a convoluted path, when AI companies have had an open invitation to sit down and negotiate for years. We have been working with government to come up with a model since 2024. We’ve come up with solutions and tech has steadfastly refused to even talk,” Pullen said.

While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law.
The Media, Entertainment & Arts Alliance said it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal, and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.
after newsletter promotion

While government MPs declined to comment on the report, senior Labor figures have recently begun more forcefully pointing to what they claim are shortfalls in copyright law in the AI age – despite major rightsholder groups rejecting the need for change. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, on Tuesday said “the status quo is no good” for creative workers, a line repeated by the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, on Thursday. Marles added on News24: “People are being ripped off”.
The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.
“Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland said.
“The Government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”
Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.
The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.
“This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”
Pocock also described it as “some sort of divide and conquer strategy”.

“It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young urged the government not to meet copyright demands requested by big tech.
“What they’re asking Australia to do actually is to undermine copyright the world over. Australia will become known as the Cayman Islands for AI if we allow this loophole to happen,” she told News24.
“I say, don’t be that stupid. Stand up to them.”

articles.title: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message
articles.summary:
Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall

  • Get our breaking…
articles.byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.
The research, published in the journal Science Advances, involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.

The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.

blocks.caption: A gravimeter, set up in a men’s bathroom, was used to detect the position of an elevator counterweight, enabling scientists to transmit a message. Photograph: Andrew Groszek/University of Queensland

blocks.text: The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.

The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics, in a statement. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”

Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.

To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.
According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.
after newsletter promotion

The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.

Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.”
“Quantum sensors are still under development,” Davis said.
“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side,” he added. “It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”

Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed, “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.
The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment, which began in 1927.

articles.title: Senator-judges ask why defense witness weighing in on report he hasn't read
articles.summary: Senator-judges cast doubt on the capability of a defense witness to answer questions about a report detailing Duterte"s alleged unexplained wealth, especially since he didn't read it.

blocks.text: Senator-judges cast doubt on the capability of a defense witness to answer questions about a report detailing Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth, especially after it was revealed that he did not read the report at all.

At Duterte's impeachment trial on Thursday, defense counsel Mark Vinluan presented AML (Anti-Money Laundering) Consulting PH head Rainer Dela Fuente, asking him about the findings of prosecution witness Alexander Cabrera.
Cabrera, a financial forensic analyst, presented a report alleging that Duterte had unexplained wealth amounting to at least P817 million.
Much of Vinluan’s questioning referred to Cabrera’s report, repeatedly calling Cabrera a “so-called expert.”
“In financial investigations, how important is it to meticulously go through the records one by one, instead of considering summaries based on mere conjectures?” Vinuluan.
Dela Fuente said that it was very important, saying that deviations could cast doubt on computations.
“We cannot base, especially if it concerns financial investigations, it is not just based on conductures, There should be facts,” Dela Fuente said in a mix of English and Filipino.
However, Vinluan’s line of questioning also strayed to other matters.
In one instance, Vinluan showed Dela Fuente a photo of a P13.5 million Benz G-Wagon and asked him what he thought of a politician who owned such a car.
“I’d rather not answer that,” Dela Fuente said.

A few questions later, Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo spoke up, asking Senate Impeachment presiding officer Francis Escudero to put the witness on a shorter leash and asking about his qualifications to testify on the matter.

Senator-judge Joel Villanueva also raised that Dela Fuente's subpoena only asked that he was there for his expertise in AML and related matters. He asked Escudero if Dela Fuente was there to refute Cabrera’s report.
“Did you give the witness a copy of the forensic report?” Villanueva asked Vinluan.
“No, Your Honor,” Vinluan replied. He further justified that the defense did not want to have prior correspondence with the defense witness.
“If he is to refute the report then he should have seen the report,” Villanueva said.
Tulfo echoed Villanueva’s sentiment.
“In the first place, wala siyang ideya kung ano yung nakasaad sa sinabi ng testigo… dapat beforehand, he was given a copy of those documents para mapag-aralan niya,” Tulfo said.
(In the first place, he does not have an idea on what is said by the witness… it should have been beforehand, he was given a copy of those documents so he could study it.)
Tulfo asked why even the ownership of a G-Wagon was raised.
“Ano ito, salesman na rin?” he added.
(What is he? A salesman?)
Senator-judge Bam Aquino also questioned Dela Fuente, asking if none of the financial and bank records subpoenaed by the impeachment court was shown to him.
Dela Fuente could be heard off-camera saying “none.”

“It’s really concepts and general ideas about AMLA [AML Act] and financial investigations? Okay, Mr. Witness, and again, hindi mo ito kasalanan, but many times we have witnesses here, pag tinatanong namin, ang sinasagot namin, ‘Hindi ho namin alam’. So gusto amin ng mga witness na pwede kami sagutin dirtso talaga,” Aquino said.
(This is not your fault, but many times we've had witnesses here, and when we ask them questions, they reply 'We don't know.' So we want a witness who can give us direct answers.)
During Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros’ interjection, Dela Fuente said that he still respected Cabrera but maintained that the law should be followed.

“Ang ginagawa ko lang ho, binabangga ang kanyang ginawa sa kung ano yung mayroon sa batas. Kung ito po ay maga-align, yun ang aking role dito… I don’t need to read the full report going here because kahit i-flash yan ngayon palang, makikita niyo na po, aligned ba ito sa provisions ng AMLA?” Dela Fuente said.

(What I did here was compare what he did on what is in the law, if this was aligned, that is what my role is… I don’t need to read the full report going here because even if it is flashed just now, you can see it now, is it aligned with AMLA?) — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Wadephul: 'Coalition of the Willing' talks in Berlin send strong signal to Moscow
articles.summary: German Foreign Minister Wadephul has said the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin sends a clear message to Moscow to take peace talks seriously. He also warned Ukraine should be prepared for…

image.caption: Wadephul said Germany was also prepared for US-led peace talks to fail Image: DW

blocks.text: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday's meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin sent a strong signal to Moscow that it was time to take negotiations to end the war in Ukraine seriously.

Speaking to DW during a visit to the South Caucasus, Wadephul described the summit as the largest meeting of Ukraine's supporters so far. The meeting represents the 18th set of high-level talks among the coalition's members.

He said it demonstrated that allies remained firmly behind Kyiv in the fifth year of Russia's war and were ready to do "what was necessary to ensure Ukraine could negotiate from a position of strength."
"The summit itself is already a success," he told DW.

blocks.caption: The so-called coalition of the willing is meeting in Berlin to discuss further aid to UkraineImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Wadephul also welcomed the US initiative to restart peace negotiations. After nine months without progress, an initial meeting had taken place in Abu Dhabi, with a follow-up round planned and European participation expected.
Wadephul promises future support for Ukraine

"We are also preparing for the possibility that the negotiations will not be successful and that, over the coming winter, we will have to continue supplying Ukraine with heating, electricity and all essential supplies, including water," he said.
"And we will continue to stand by Ukraine militarily."
He stressed that any peace agreement must include security guarantees to protect Ukraine against future Russian attacks.
In earlier comments during his trip to the South Caucasus, Wadephul said that Ukraine and Europe must be involved in any negotiations over the future of Ukraine.
Wadephul did, however, welcome the trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
"Every conversation that takes place is a good conversation," he told DW during a visit to Azerbaijan on Wednesday.
Later on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said he had invited Europeans to Moscow for talks on the potential structure of future talks to end the war.

articles.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
articles.summary: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft…

image.caption: Protestors at the COP31 in Antalya Turkey calling for a phaseout of fossil fuels, the burning of which is the main driver of climate changeImage: DW

blocks.text: Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations with representatives from nearly 200 countries on issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
The text also includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that had been pushed by host Turkey.

blocks.caption: COP31 negotiators are once again gearing up to fight to have fossil fuels mentioned in a final decision in the yearly UN climate summitImage: Dilara Senkaya/REUTERS

blocks.text: It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries. But it did link the target to efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally alongside other energy efficiency measures.
What else is in the draft text?

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.
It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane. The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?
The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up — those technologies are as yet largely unproven at scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."

"It is actively more regressive, stripping out hard-won accountability, timelines, and legal anchors just as frontline communities in the Global South are paying the steepest price for climate breakdown," said Singh in a statement.
Talks in crunch time
The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run overtime. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.
Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.
On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demand for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate the potent greenhouse gas methane.
The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

blocks.caption: A glacier collapse linked to planetary heating killed thousands in Nepal in AugustImage: Francis Mascarenhas/REUTERS

blocks.text: The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

It's the first conference taking place with the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.
More to come…

articles.title: Venezuela signs military deal with US less than a year after Maduro's ouster
articles.summary: The US Secretary of Defence says Venezuela has 'gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner'.

blocks.text: The United States and Venezuela have re-established military ties less than a year after US forces seized the then-leader of the South American country, Nicolás Maduro, in a raid on the capital, Caracas.
The interim government led by Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice-president, signed a military co-operation agreement with US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on Wednesday.
Few details about the deal have been released so far but Hegseth said that Venezuela had "gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner" in less than 12 months.
Interim President Rodríguez said the deal would help confront "common threats".
Military co-operation between the two countries was terminated in 2005 by Hugo Chávez, Venezuela's left-wing president at the time.
Chávez alleged that US military personnel sent to Venezuela to train their counterparts had made disparaging remarks about his government.
He also accused the US military office located in Fuerte Tiuna, Venezuela's largest military complex, of being "an organ of the CIA... conspiring against the government".
Under Nicolás Maduro, who succeeded Chávez after the latter's death from cancer, relations between the two countries deteriorated further.
They reached rock bottom late last year when the US doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro's capture to $50m (£38m) and eventually seized him on 3 January in a military raid.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now in custody in New York on charges of drug-trafficking and conspiracy to commit torture, which they deny.
Hegseth addressed the change in the two countries' relationship since Maduro was seized in his speech at the US embassy in Caracas on Wednesday.
"It's a great honour to be here as the first United States Secretary of War this century to set foot in Venezuela. The weight of this moment does not escape me," he said.

"Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable," he added before recalling a public appearance by then-President Maduro which had angered the Trump administration.

"Exactly one year ago today, the indicted narco-terrorist fugitive Nicolás Maduro, the man who spent more than a decade handing Venezuela's borders and territory to terrorists from all over the world, stood on a stage, not too far from here, and yelled mockingly: 'Come and get me!'. Well, we answered that call."
Hegseth added that the result of the US military raid on 3 January had been as Maduro predicted, quoting the deposed leader's words: "No war, yes peace."

He described the deal signed by him and Venezuela's defence minister on Wednesday as a "new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan military and for the Western Hemisphere through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition".
Rodríguez described it as "extraordinarily relevant for our bilateral relations".

"In a matter of months, secretary, we have turned very difficult moments for our people into a space for co-operation and mutual benefit for both of our countries," she said addressing Hegseth during a meeting at the presidential palace.

While no details of the deal have been published, in her speech Rodríguez mentioned the training of Venezuela's armed forces and improving its "operational equipment" and access to new technology "to confront shared threats".

In his speech at the US embassy, Hegseth was more direct about who he considers to be those threats. Addressing "the narco-terrorists who abuse this [Venezuela] as a safe haven", he warned that "we will hunt you down, we will find you, and we will kill you".
From Venezuela, Hegseth travelled on to neighbouring Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration.
Colombia is already part of the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition and in August, Hegseth had floated the possibility of joint US-Colombian military operations against armed groups.
On Wednesday, President de la Espriella took to X to deny a report by the New York Times which had stated that he had rejected carrying out joint operations, external.
In his post, he stressed that any decision would be taken while respecting Colombia's constitution, and the country's laws and sovereignty.
Hegseth reposted the tweet commenting that the US-Colombian partnership "is stronger than ever before".

articles.title: Pakistan minister to visit India, but no breakthrough expected
articles.summary: A Pakistani minister's visit to India for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization forum marks a rare high-level contact between the two archrivals, but analysts say it does not signal a resumption of…

image.caption: It's the first India visit by a Pakistani federal minister since the two neighbors fought a four-day conflict last yearImage: Aman Sharma/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will travel to India from November 20 to 22 to participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue in New Delhi.
It marks the first India visit by a Pakistani federal minister since the two nuclear-armed archrivals fought a four-day war last year.

The fighting erupted after armed gunmen killed over two dozen tourists, mostly Hindus, in India-administered Kashmir in April 2025. New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack, a charge Pakistan denied.
Since the military confrontation, diplomatic tensions have remained high, leaving little room for official engagement between the two sides.
The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO summit in Tianjin in September 2025.
As the forum's host, India has invited all member states to participate in the event.
The SCO is a political, economic, and security alliance established in 2001. Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan are its current members.

blocks.caption: Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Civilizational Dialogue in New DelhiImage: Dogukan Keskinkilic/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 'good sign'

Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, sees significance in the fact that neither side sought to avoid the engagement. "The real takeaway is that the relationship isn't so broken that India won't invite Pakistan, or that Pakistan won't come. That alone is a good sign," he told DW.
But Bisaria cautions against assuming that the invitation followed a diplomatic breakthrough.

"The trigger was procedural. This forum grew out of Modi's proposal at the 2025 SCO summit in Tianjin, and as host, New Delhi invited every SCO member. I see no evidence of a back channel or outside mediation, and I wouldn't read much into that either way," he said.
'Being pragmatic'
The multilateral setting serves both countries, though for different reasons.

Pakistan wants to retain its influence within the organization. It currently holds the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026–27 and is due to host the next leaders' summit in Islamabad in August 2027.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, argues that Islamabad's decision to send a senior minister should be understood primarily in terms of its position in the grouping.

"Pakistan is keen to maintain its position and influence within the SCO and does not want to relinquish its role in the organization. The minister's visit should therefore be seen primarily in the context of Pakistan fulfilling its commitments under the SCO Charter, rather than as a gesture towards India," Siddiqa told DW.
A 'frozen conflict': India-Pakistan tensions persist
T C A Raghavan, another former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, shares a similar sentiment.

"Both India and Pakistan attach importance to the SCO, and Pakistan currently holds its chairmanship. This visit should be seen primarily in the context of the SCO, rather than as a development in India-Pakistan bilateral relations," Raghavan told DW.

"Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. There will be no real impact on the India-Pakistan bilateral."
The bilateral freeze
Since the April 2025 attack, India has maintained that terrorism and talks cannot go hand in hand.

"Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place. There has been no change," Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Foreign Ministry, said at the end of October.
Pakistan, meanwhile, continues to raise the issues of Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty, which New Delhi placed "in abeyance" following the attack.

Malik, the climate change minister traveling to India, has been a prominent voice in Pakistan's campaign over water rights. In June, he warned: "We will protect ourselves... if anyone lays a hand over our share of water, we'll cut off that hand."
Sanjay Kumar Bhardwaj, professor at the Center for South Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the SCO is part of India's "multi-aligned foreign policy."
He noted that the forum "doesn't provide any space to normalize relations with Pakistan."

blocks.caption: The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra ModiImage: Pyotr Kovalev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Unofficial channels, no formal dialogue
The absence of official talks, however, does not mean all bilateral communication has stopped.

Since the May 2025 confrontation, Indian and Pakistani former diplomats, strategic experts, parliamentarians and retired military officers have reportedly taken part in a series of informal or semi-official back-channel meetings.
Such exchanges allow participants to assess the other side's thinking, keep informal lines of communication open and reduce the risk of miscalculation.
But they do not amount to formal negotiations. New Delhi has said retired officials attending such meetings do so in their personal capacities.

An assessment by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in November said both governments appeared reluctant to resume secret talks, despite the role earlier back-channel contacts had played in stabilizing relations.
Bisaria described the visit by a Pakistani minister to India as "a modest step forward, not a breakthrough."
What happens next, he said, "depends on Pakistan."

"If it avoids grandstanding in Delhi and offers credible assurances on terrorism, publicly or quietly, it becomes more likely that Indian leaders will attend next year's SCO summit in Islamabad. That will be the real test."

articles.title: Sara Duterte's defense fails to challenge evidence in impeachment trial
articles.summary: With the conclusion of the 44th day of Vice President Sara Duterte"s impeachment trial, the House prosecution said that her defense team has yet to debunk the evidence against her.

blocks.text: Published November 19, 2026 9:24pm
With the conclusion of the 44th day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, the House prosecution said that her defense team has yet to debunk the evidence against her.

In a press briefing after the trial, House prosecution panel adviser Ace Barbers said that AML (Anti-Money Laundering) Consulting PH founder Rainer Dela Fuente did not have the experience to qualify him to answer questions.

“Hanggang ngayon (Until now), with this latest witness that they presented before the impeachment court, they have not debunked, refuted, nor disputed all the evidence and testimonies of our witnesses that we presented before the court,” Barbers said.

“The defense was consistent in presenting evidence or witnesses that did not support the defense of their principal but rather, just what I mentioned last week, talagang nilulubog sa kumunoy o hinulog sa sinkhole (sinking in quicksand or falling into a sinkhole),” he added.

Other than the prosecution, senator-judges also raised concerns about Dela Fuente’s capacity to answer questions and to debunk an earlier report that accused Duterte of having P817 million in unexplained wealth.
Meanwhile, House Prosecutor Chel Diokno, who cross-examined Dela Fuente earlier, said that he would not comment on the proceedings themselves.
However, Diokno admitted that he was surprised to find out that Dela Fuente did not read any of the financial records at all.

“As a lawyer, I think that is really a basic requirement that before anyone can render an opinion, especially an alleged expert dapat alam niya 'yung facts. Dapat nabasa niya 'yung pertinent documents... Kung ganun, ano kaya ang magiging weight ng kanyang sinasabi? And that was one of the things that we pointed out sa cross kanina,” Diokno said.

(As a lawyer, I think that is really a basic requirement that before anyone can render an opinion, especially an alleged expert, he should know the facts. He should have read the pertinent documents… If so, what would be the weight of what he says? And that was one of the things that we pointed out during cross earlier.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.summary: Dozens of people were missing on Thursday after a boat carrying migrants bound for Europe capsized off the coast of Senegal, a local non-governmental organization said, in the latest incident along…

image.caption: The remains of a boat lie on the shore following an accident at sea involving migrants off the coast of Yenne, Senegal, on Thursday. (Misper Apawu/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Dozens of people were missing on Thursday after a boat carrying migrants bound for Europe capsized off the coast of Senegal, a local non-governmental organization said, in the latest incident along the West Africa route.
Nearly 600 people have died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year

Nearly 600 people have died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year, the UN refugee agency known as UNHCR said this week. Traffic has intensified this month, as sea conditions became calmer and more favourable for crossings.

More than 8,000 people arrived at the Canary Islands in the first 12 days of November, tripling the number of arrivals recorded in all of November last year and hitting the highest monthly level since October 2023, UNHCR said.

The journeys from Senegal and neighbouring countries on rickety boats are often perilous, resulting in dozens of deaths despite authorities' efforts to intercept them. Earlier this month, a sinking north of Dakar near the town of Kébémer killed more than 40 people.

The latest incident occurred overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday off the coast of Yenne, a town south of the capital Dakar, and one death had been confirmed as of Thursday morning, French radio reported.
"There was a survivor who said there were around 50 people aboard," Adama Mbengue, president of Action for Human Rights and ​Friendship, told Reuters.

items: Death toll rises to 39 after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal
Children among at least 139 dead after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti coast

blocks.text: Following the earlier sinking near Kébémer, President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said on X that his government would "fight against those who organize these crossings" and try to "provide our youth with reasons to have hope here at home."

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Faye requested a detailed report on the challenges to curbing irregular migration and stressed the need to improve youth employment prospects, according to a government statement.
Life jackets are seen inside the boat. (Misper Apawu/Reuters)

Earlier in the week, UNHCR called for urgent action to save lives along migration routes and Patrick Eba, deputy director of the agency's Division of International Protection and Solutions, said that job creation in West Africa would help reduce fatalities at sea.
"We are failing to give people opportunities and options where they are," he said.
"These are people who are not fleeing war or persecution. Migrants across this region are searching for opportunities that they cannot find in their own countries."

articles.title: Defense witness grilled over ‘useless’ testimony
articles.summary: Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente cites confidentiality to explain why he did not review prosecution witness Alex Cabrera's forensic report, prompting criticisms from several senator-judges

blocks.text: EXPERT. Defense witness Rainer Dela Fuente testifies on Day 44 of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial on November 19, 2026.
Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente cites confidentiality to explain why he did not review prosecution witness Alex Cabrera's forensic report, prompting criticisms from several senator-judges

items: Defense witness Rainer Dela Fuente admitted he had not read the prosecution's financial forensic report or its supporting documents before testifying in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Dela Fuente's lack of review raised concerns among senator-judges about the validity of his testimony, with some questioning how he could refute the report's findings without having seen the underlying documents.

The prosecution challenged Dela Fuente's qualifications and expertise, emphasizing the importance of context in evaluating financial reports, particularly in light of allegations of unexplained wealth against Duterte.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A defense witness admitted that he had not read the prosecution’s financial forensic report or reviewed its supporting documents before testifying in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday, November 19.
Lawyer Rainer Dela Fuente, a former Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) financial investigator, was presented as an expert witness for the defense on Day 44 of the trial.
During his direct examination, defense lawyer Mark Vinluan sought to challenge the methodology and findings of the financial forensic report prepared by prosecution witness Alex Cabrera.

blocks.caption: Financial analyst tells impeach court: Sara Duterte has P817M in undisclosed wealth

blocks.text: Dela Fuente, however, told the impeachment court that he had not been provided copies of the report and its supporting documents before the hearing.

“No, Your Honor,” Dela Fuente said when asked whether he had received copies of AMLC records, bank statements, insurance placements, and general information sheets (GIS) of companies linked to Duterte.
Vinluan confirmed that the witness had not reviewed the entire report, saying the defense intended to focus on specific portions of the 50-page document.
“If he is to refute the report, then he should have seen the report, should have read the report,” Senator-judge Joel Villanueva said.
“Now if he cannot answer these questions then, for me, it’s going to be useless,” Villanueva added.
Other senator-judges, including Erwin Tulfo, also questioned how Dela Fuente could examine the report’s findings without reviewing the underlying documents.

“Kung hindi naman niya po nakita pala ay mga dokumento, STRs (Suspicious Transaction Reports), CTRs (Covered Transaction Reports), what good is it? Para anong tetestigo niya, eh puro ito theory sa kanyang paningin, sa kanyang paniniwala,” Tulfo said.
(If has has not seen the documents, STRs, CTRs, what good is it? What’s his testimony for, it’ll just be all his theory, his beliefs.)
He added: “The witnesses you’ve been presenting here these past few days are weak. Get somebody who can really stand up, who can really answer questions from the senator-judges.”
Dela Fuente was listed as a defense witness who would testify on fundamental legal concepts under the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA).

Explaining why he did not review the report and its supporting documents, Dela Fuente cited confidentiality concerns. He also said he was not dismissing Cabrera’s findings but was merely answering the defense’s hypothetical questions based on his understanding of the law.

“Ang akin lang pong saligan ay ang ating AMLA, ang ating batas, so I can answer based on the law… Ako personally, ayoko basahin yung report because coming here, and wala rin ako access sa report, coming here and reading that report, I will develop biases,” Dela Fuente said.

(My only basis is our AMLA, and our laws, so I can answer based on the law… Personally, I don’t want to read the report because coming here, and I also did not have access to the report, coming here here and reading that report, I will develop biases.)
The prosecution tried to paint Dela Fuente as unqualified.

“Your claimed expertise as a financial expert in financial investigation only comes from the 25 months that you were an entry-level investigator for the AMLC. Is that correct?” Diokno asked Dela Fuente, who answered in the affirmative.

Dela Fuente also admitted that he was not challenging the accuracy or truthfulness of the AMLC reports, Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records, and bank records involving the Vice President.
Diokno, like the senators, also made a big deal of the fact that Dela Fuente did not read the forensic examination report prepared by the prosecution’s witness, Alexander Cabrera.

“Let’s say that I were going to evaluate your investigation report,” Diokno said. “If in my evaluation, I decide not to read everything and pick portions only, don’t you think it will be unfair to you?”
“You didn’t read the whole report. Wouldn’t you agree that context means a lot in terms of evaluating the veracity of a financial report?” Diokno added.

Cabrera previously testified that based on his analysis of the Vice President’s bank and financial records, Duterte, and her husband, Mans Carpio, had accumulated P817 million unexplained wealth from 2022 to 2025.
Duterte is being tried for Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth. – with reports from Dwight de Leon/Rappler.com
